final.value_proposition: A differentiated marine‑coating kit marketed as "premium, durable marine coating for home exterior projects," leveraging Jotun’s marine expertise to deliver superior protection and color retention, positioned as a trusted professional‑grade
final.next_action: Execute the 10‑week, €15,000 online conjoint survey with 500 respondents, measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay for the premium kit.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer perception of marine coatings as premium or professional trust. The test will resolve this.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.

Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users with a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product into a broader B2B market (e.g., corporate wellness programs, senior centers).
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B segments.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited via a panel of adults aged 25-55 in Japan (reflecting 1993 demographic). They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) receive a description of a home body-fat analyzer with a price of ¥15,000 (approx. $130 in 1993 dollars) and are asked if they would purchase it; (B) receive the same description plus a statement that insurance would reimburse the cost. The primary outcome is the proportion of participants who indicate intent to purchase in each condition. Secondary
X1.sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) to detect a 10 percentage point difference with 80% power and a 5% significance level.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs. "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (open-ended).

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for weight‑management versus status‑signaling messaging. frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users with a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product into a broader B2B market (e.g., corporate wellness programs, senior centers).
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B segments.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyzer if they perceive it as a reliable, easy‑to‑use tool for weight management, and they are willing to pay a premium for accuracy.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to monitor body composition for health and weight control; Tanita would benefit by capturing premium sales.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers trust the device provides accurate, actionable data, they will purchase it for personal use, shifting from clinic/health club use to home use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device at a higher price point directly to consumers, generating higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Consumers in 1993 have sufficient disposable income to afford a premium home scale.
There is a market segment willing to purchase a body‑fat analyzer for personal use.
Marketing can effectively communicate accuracy and ease of use to this segment.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% above the price of standard bathroom scales for a body‑fat analyzer.
Pilot sales of a consumer‑branded model will exceed 5,000 units within 12 weeks if positioned as a health tool.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view the device as a visible marker of health commitment, they will purchase it to signal personal achievement and social status, even if the core health benefit is secondary.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would price the device at a premium and sell it directly to consumers, leveraging brand association with health and status to justify higher margins.
assumptions: Consumers in 1993 value social signaling of health status.
There is a segment willing to pay for a device that conveys prestige.
Marketing can effectively communicate status value and health benefits.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% above the price of standard bathroom scales for a status‑branded body‑fat analyzer.
Pilot sales of a consumer‑branded model will exceed 3,000 units within 12 weeks if positioned as a status symbol for health‑conscious individuals.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a home body-fat analyzer emphasizing either weight management accuracy (T1) or status signaling (T2). They are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent. The test also collects demographic data.
X1.sample: 500 health‑conscious adults aged 25‑55 in Japan and the U.S., recruited via online panels. Stratify by gender and income to reflect 1993 demographics.
X1.measure: Average WTP (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale). Secondary: self‑reported primary motivation (accuracy vs status).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Average WTP for status‑focused version will be at least 20% above the standard scale price. Purchase intent will be at least 30% for the status version.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Corporate Purchase Intent Test (or a similar survey) to measure actual purchase intent before committing resources. If the test shows consumer purchase intent above 30% (justifying a home consumer line), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain focus on B2B clinic/health club‑ ‑ ‑

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users with a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product into a broader B2B market (e.g., corporate wellness programs, senior centers).
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B segments.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.

T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking to monitor body composition for personal health and fitness.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers respond to medical evidence linking excess body fat to health risks and seek affordable, convenient methods to track progress.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device directly to consumers at a premium price, capturing margin through sales and potential subscription services for data tracking.
assumptions: Consumers trust medical evidence linking body fat to health outcomes.
Consumers are willing to invest in home health monitoring devices.
Price sensitivity is manageable for the target segment.
predictions: If offered at a price point below €200, purchase intent among health-conscious consumers will be above 15% in a survey.
Repeat purchase rate for subscription services will be higher among those who use the device regularly.
T1.first_claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyzer if they perceive it as a reliable, easy-to-use tool for weight management and can afford the price.

T2.claim: Employers and health insurance providers will adopt a home body-fat analyzer as part of wellness programs and reimbursement, driving bulk purchases and subscription models.
T2.who_benefits: Corporate wellness programs, health insurance companies, and employees seeking health benefits.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Employers and insurers respond to rising health costs and regulatory pressure to promote preventive care; they seek cost-effective tools to monitor employee health and reduce claims.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell devices at volume discounts and offer subscription services for data analytics, earning recurring revenue from corporate contracts and insurance partnerships.
assumptions: Corporate wellness programs are expanding and seek measurable health metrics.
Health insurers are willing to reimburse home health monitoring devices as part of preventive care.
Price sensitivity for bulk purchases is lower than for individual consumers.
predictions: If offered at a bulk price of €150 per unit, corporate buyers will place orders for at least 50 devices within 12 weeks.
Insurance reimbursement for home body-fat analysis will increase when demonstrated to reduce claim costs.

X1.name: Consumer vs Corporate Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Health‑conscious consumers (n=200) and (B) Corporate wellness program managers (n=200). Each participant views a product description of a home body‑fat analyzer priced at €180 (just below the €200 threshold). They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal use?" (binary yes/no). Additionally, for corporate group, they are asked: "Would you place an order for 50 devices for your wellness program?" (binary yes/no).
X1.sample: 400 adults: 200 health‑conscious consumers recruited via consumer panels, 200 corporate wellness managers recruited via professional networks.
X1.measure: Purchase intent for consumers (percentage saying yes) and corporate order intent (percentage saying yes).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer purchase intent ≥ 30% (justifies home consumer proposition). Corporate order intent ≤ 10% (supports B2B focus).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Consumer purchase intent ≤ 20% (low demand for home use). Corporate order intent ≥ 25% (warranting corporate partnership).

X1.decision_rule: If consumer purchase intent ≥ 30% → proceed with home consumer proposition. If corporate order intent ≥ 25% → explore corporate partnership. If both conditions met, consider dual‑track approach. If neither met, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or corporate adoption. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Corporate Purchase Intent Test (or a similar survey) to measure actual purchase intent before committing resources. If the test shows consumer purchase intent above 30% (justifying a home consumer line), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain focus on B2B clinic/health club‑  ‑
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious consumers seeking weight management and fitness tracking, and corporate wellness programs seeking measurable health metrics.
final.value_proposition: A home body‑fat analyzer that provides reliable, easy‑to‑use data for personal health monitoring, sold directly at a premium price and supported by subscription services.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer vs Corporate Purchase Intent Test (or a similar survey) with 400 participants (200 health‑conscious consumers, 200 corporate wellness managers) to measure purchase intent and order intent, respectively.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and corporate adoption in 1993. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows consumer purchase intent above 30% (justifying a home consumer line).
If the test shows corporate order intent above 25% (warranting a corporate partnership).

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (Test X1) to measure willingness to pay for a health-focused home body-fat analyzer before committing resources. If the survey shows a premium of at least 15% for the health description, proceed with a health-focused consumer proposition; otherwise, consider other options or no expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users with a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product into a broader B2B market (e.g., corporate wellness programs, senior centers).
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B segments.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyzer if they perceive it as a reliable, easy‑to‑use tool for weight management, and they are willing to pay a premium for accuracy.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to monitor body composition for health and weight control; Tanita would benefit by capturing premium pricing and repeat purchases of accessories.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of body‑fat percentage as a health indicator (e.g., heart disease, diabetes) combined with the convenience of a stand‑on device will motivate individuals to purchase a home analyzer.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device at a higher price point and potentially offer consumables (e.g., measurement strips) or subscription services for data tracking.
assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a valid method for body‑fat measurement.
There is sufficient disposable income among target consumers to afford a premium home scale.
Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits and ease of use.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% above the price of standard bathroom scales for a body‑fat analyzer.
Pilot sales of a consumer‑branded home model will exceed 5,000 units within 12 weeks if positioned as a health tool.
T1.first_claim: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyzer if they perceive it as a reliable, easy‑to‑use tool for weight management, and they are willing to pay a premium for accuracy.

T2.claim: Fitness‑oriented consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyzer if they view it as a performance‑enhancing tool that provides actionable data for training and competition, and they are willing to pay a premium for real‑time feedback.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers who engage in regular exercise and track performance; Tanita would benefit by selling devices at premium prices and offering subscription services for data analysis.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing popularity of fitness culture and the desire for measurable, immediate feedback on training effectiveness will motivate consumers to purchase a home device that provides body‑fat and performance metrics.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device at a higher price point and offer optional subscription services for data visualization, coaching insights, or integration with fitness apps.
assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a valid method for measuring body composition.
There is a segment of consumers willing to invest in fitness technology beyond basic equipment.
Marketing can highlight the device’s real‑time performance data as a competitive advantage.
predictions: Surveyed fitness consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% above the price of standard bathroom scales for a device that provides body‑fat and performance metrics.
Pilot sales of a fitness‑focused home model will exceed 3,000 units within 12 weeks if positioned as a training tool.
T2.first_claim: Fitness‑oriented consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyzer if they view it as a performance‑enhancing tool that provides actionable data for training and competition, and they are willing to pay a premium for real‑time feedback.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a portable 406 MHz distress beacon because the technology provides a reliable, long-range distress signal that is easier to use than traditional emergency radio or GPS devices.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, campers) who frequently travel in remote areas and need a safety device that can be activated quickly and is visible to search and rescue teams.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If a consumer distress beacon is easy to carry, requires no battery charging, and can be activated with a single button press, they will choose it over cumbersome radio or GPS devices because it reduces setup time and increases confidence
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon directly to consumers through online channels or outdoor retailers, capturing the full consumer price margin while leveraging its existing 406 MHz technology and regulatory compliance.
assumptions: Consumers in 2002 are aware of the existence of personal locator beacons and understand their benefits.
They trust the reliability of the 406 MHz frequency for distress signaling.
Price sensitivity is moderate, allowing a premium for a reliable safety device.
predictions: A survey of outdoor recreationists will show willingness to pay at least $300 for a portable 406 MHz distress beacon.
Purchase intent will be higher when the beacon is presented as a single-button, emergency-only device compared to a multi-feature GPS device.

X1.name: Consumer vs Emergency Responder Preference Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase scenarios.
X1.sample: 200 respondents: 100 outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, campers) and 100 emergency responders/SAR team members.
X1.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a 406 MHz distress beacon described as a single-button, portable device for emergency use only. Respondents indicate maximum price they would pay and which scenario they prefer (outdoor recreation or emergency responder).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreationists will show a WTP of at least $300 and will choose the outdoor recreation scenario over the emergency responder scenario.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency responders will show a WTP of at least $300 and will choose the emergency responder scenario over the outdoor recreation scenario.

X1.decision_rule: If outdoor recreationists' average WTP ≥ $300 and prefer the outdoor recreation scenario → T1 is supported. If emergency responders' average WTP ≥ $300 and prefer the emergency responder scenario → T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories are rejected.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed choice-based conjoint survey (Test X1) to test whether outdoor recreationists would adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon and are willing to pay a premium price. If the survey confirms willingness to pay at least $300 and prefer the outdoor recreation scenario, proceed to develop a consumer product; otherwise, maintain the current B2B
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, campers) who frequently travel in remote areas and need a safety device that can be activated quickly and is visible to search and rescue teams.
final.value_proposition: A portable, single-button 406 MHz distress beacon that provides reliable, long-range distress signaling, reducing setup time and increasing confidence compared to traditional emergency radio or GPS devices.
final.next_action: Run Test X1 (online choice-based conjoint survey) with 200 respondents (100 outdoor recreationists, 100 emergency responders) to measure willingness to pay and purchase preference.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a 406 MHz distress beacon in 2002.
would_change_if: If the survey shows outdoor recreationists' average willingness to pay < $300 or prefer the emergency responder scenario, we would abandon T1 and focus on B2B/B2G markets.
If new evidence shows strong demand from emergency responders for a standardized 406 MHz beacon, we would shift to supporting T2.

result.question: It is late 2002. Should ACR Electronics develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology? What evidence would justify that investment?
result.brief: ACR Electronics is a Fort Lauderdale maker of emergency radio beacons for ships and aircraft and of survival lights for military and commercial marine users. You have not been told how far it already reaches individual buyers, so find out. You are an outside analyst working only from public sources. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Many sources were written after the decision date: reason only from what was knowable on that date, and do not use what you may know about later events. Financial data is not in the dossier, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. arguments.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Emergency Responder Preference Test
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase scenarios.
arguments.sample: 200 respondents: 100 outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, campers) and 100 emergency responders/SAR team members.
arguments.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a 406 MHz distress beacon described as a single-button, portable device for emergency use only. Respondents indicate maximum price they would pay and which scenario they prefer (outdoor recreation or emergency responder).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreationists will show a WTP of at least $300 and will choose the outdoor recreation scenario over the emergency responder scenario.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency responders will show a WTP of at least $300 and will choose the emergency responder scenario over the outdoor recreation scenario.

arguments.decision_rule: If outdoor recreationists' average WTP ≥ $300 and prefer the outdoor recreation scenario → T1 is supported. If emergency responders' average WTP ≥ $300 and prefer the emergency responder scenario → T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories are rejected.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.target_customer: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, campers) who frequently travel in remote areas and need a safety device that can be activated quickly and is visible to search and rescue teams.
arguments.value_proposition: A portable, single-button 406 MHz distress beacon that provides reliable, long-range distress signaling, reducing setup time and increasing confidence compared to traditional emergency radio or GPS devices.
arguments.next_action: Run Test X1 (online choice-based conjoint survey) with 200 respondents (100 outdoor recreationists, 100 emergency responders) to measure willingness to pay and purchase preference.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a 406 MHz distress beacon in 2002.
would_change_if: If the survey shows outdoor recreationists' average willingness to pay < $300 or prefer the emergency responder scenario, we would abandon T1 and focus on B2B/B2G markets.
If new evidence shows strong demand from emergency responders for a standardized 406 MHz beacon, we would shift to supporting T2.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer product yet. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a 406 MHz distress beacon among outdoor recreationists. If the survey meets the decision thresholds (purchase intent ≥30% and mean WTP ≥€250), proceed to develop a consumer product; otherwise, abandon consumer expansion and focus on B2B/B2G markets.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, long-range emergency communication solution that complements existing safety gear.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, boaters) who need a backup distress signal beyond cell phone or radio range.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users already carry survival gear and are willing to invest in safety equipment; a distress beacon that works with satellites and is easy to activate adds a credible safety layer without compromising existing gear.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon directly to consumers through online channels and outdoor retailers, capturing the full retail price; volume sales can be leveraged to offset certification costs.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large enough to support a consumer product.
Consumers trust satellite-based distress signals over other methods.
Distribution channels (outdoor retailers, online) are accessible to ACR.
predictions: If offered at a price point comparable to other outdoor safety gear (e.g., $200-300), purchase intent among surveyed outdoor recreationists will be at least 15% within 12 weeks.
Actual sales will exceed 5,000 units in the first year if marketing reaches the target audience.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, long-range emergency communication solution that complements existing safety gear.

T2.claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a standardized, reliable signal that can be detected across vast geographic areas, reducing response time and cost.
T2.who_benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, coast guards, and emergency response teams that need to locate distressed individuals in remote or rugged terrain.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These agencies already rely on multiple communication methods but face challenges with signal saturation, range limitations, and cost of specialized equipment. A standardized satellite distress beacon that can be tracked across large areas
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon to government agencies through procurement channels, leveraging volume sales to offset certification costs and potentially secure long-term contracts for recurring maintenance.
assumptions: Government agencies have budget for new distress equipment and prioritize standardized solutions.
406 MHz signals are detectable by existing SAR satellites and can be tracked across large areas.
Certification and compliance requirements can be met within budget.
predictions: If offered at a price point comparable to other SAR equipment (e.g., $500-1,000), purchase intent among surveyed SAR agencies will be at least 10% within 12 weeks.
Actual sales will exceed 200 units in the first year if targeted through government procurement channels.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon if it is marketed as a safety-critical emergency tool, because they prioritize safety in remote environments and are willing to pay a premium for reliable distress signaling.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) who engage in activities where emergency rescue is necessary.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users already carry safety gear and are aware of the risk of isolation; a distress beacon that uses the established 406 MHz frequency and is certified for emergency use will be perceived as a necessary addition to their kit.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through registration fees, and potentially license the technology to outdoor brands for co‑branding.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large enough to support a dedicated consumer product.
Consumers are willing to pay more for a distress beacon that is clearly labeled for emergency use.
Regulatory environment (FCC rules) permits consumer use of 406 MHz PLBs.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point above $200.
Purchase intent will be higher when the beacon is described as a safety‑critical emergency tool versus a general safety accessory.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: These agencies already operate on standardized protocols for distress signaling and rely on reliable, certified equipment. A 406 MHz beacon that meets RTCM standards and is already used by other agencies will be added to their kit lists.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon through existing B2B channels, capture volume sales, and potentially secure long‑term contracts with government agencies.
assumptions: Government procurement cycles for emergency equipment are active in 2002.
Existing 406 MHz PLBs are already used by at least one major SAR agency.
Compliance with RTCM standards is a prerequisite for procurement.
predictions: Government procurement requests for 406 MHz PLBs will increase in 2002.
Purchase intent from SAR agencies will be higher when the beacon is described as a compliant, certified emergency tool versus a consumer product.

X1.name: Consumer vs B2B Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message frames: (A) safety‑critical emergency tool for outdoor recreation (T1), (B) compliant, certified emergency tool for SAR teams (T2). Both messages describe the same 406 MHz beacon (specifications, price, registration requirements) but frame it differently. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale and willingness to pay. The test also
X1.sample: 200 U.S. adults who have participated in outdoor recreation (hiking, camping, kayaking) in the past year and 200 emergency responders/SAR personnel (firefighters, police, coast guard). Recruitment via panel providers to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) and average willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: proportion of participants who would purchase at the price point indicated.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation participants exposed to the safety‑critical frame will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than those exposed to the SAR frame.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency responders exposed to the SAR frame will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than those exposed to the safety‑critical frame.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the safety‑critical frame exceeds the SAR frame by at least 1.5 points on the 1‑10 scale AND the willingness to pay difference is at least EUR 50, then T1 is supported. If the opposite pattern holds, T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the threshold, both theories remain

final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon marketed as a safety‑critical emergency tool for remote environments, sold directly to consumers at a premium price, with recurring revenue from registration and potential licensing to outdoor brands.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 online survey test (X1) with 200 outdoor recreation participants and 200 emergency responders.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a 406 MHz distress beacon.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the safety‑critical frame is at least 1.5 points higher than the SAR frame and willingness to pay is at least €50 higher, indicating strong consumer demand.

X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults: 250 self-identified outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hiking, camping) and 250 emergency responders/search-and-rescue personnel (recruited via outdoor recreation forums and SAR agency networks).
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who would purchase the device in their assigned scenario. Secondary outcomes: average price willingness-to-pay (EUR) and perceived reliability (1-10 scale).

arguments.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon because it provides a reliable, long-range emergency communication solution that is easier to use than existing methods (e.g., satellite phones, radio).
arguments.who_benefits: Individual hikers, campers, and outdoor adventurers who need a lightweight, automatic distress signal device.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently rely on unreliable or cumbersome methods; a distress beacon that works with existing satellite networks and can be deployed without additional training would reduce risk and increase confidence in remote activities.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the device directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through registration fees, and build brand awareness among outdoor communities.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. were stable or growing in 2002.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety features that reduce risk.
Distribution channels (e.g., outdoor retailers) exist for direct-to-consumer sales.
predictions: A survey of outdoor recreation groups would show >60% would consider purchasing a 406 MHz distress beacon.
Sales of the device would be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation density (e.g., national parks, mountain ranges).

arguments.claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a standardized, reliable signal that can be detected across vast geographic areas, reducing response time and cost.
arguments.who_benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, coast guards, and emergency management organizations that need to locate and assist remote individuals quickly.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Current methods often rely on multiple frequencies and inconsistent signal strengths; a standardized 406 MHz beacon would simplify detection and coordination, leading to faster response and potentially saving lives.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the device to government agencies and NGOs at volume prices, secure long-term contracts for service contracts (e.g., registration, data transmission), and gain credibility as a reliable emergency solution.
assumptions: Government agencies budget for emergency communication upgrades in 2002.
Standardization reduces the cost of training and integration for multiple agencies.
Existing search-and-rescue operations are willing to adopt new technology if it demonstrably improves outcomes.
predictions: A survey of search-and-rescue directors would show >50% would prioritize purchasing 406 MHz beacons for their fleet.
Sales would be concentrated in regions with high search-and-rescue activity (e.g., coastlines, mountain ranges).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly increasing small‑garden households need a tool that can handle various chores; the tractor's low price and ease of use make it attractive compared to manual tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging existing relationships and avoiding the need for new retail channels.

Consumers trust Deere's brand for agricultural equipment and will extend that trust to lawn and garden products.
predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn and garden tractor, dealers will order sufficient units to meet demand within 12 weeks.

X1.sample: 500 homeowners with small gardens (household income $20,000‑$40,000, self‑reported ownership of a lawn or garden area).
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7‑point scale (1: Very unlikely to buy; 7: Very likely to buy). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate whether homeowners prioritize inexpensive practicality over convenience. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.claim: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for a variety of chores, and easy to maintain.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain a versatile tool that reduces chore time and cost; Deere gains new revenue from consumer sales and brand extension.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly increasing demand for garden tractors indicates that homeowners are willing to purchase a product that solves multiple gardening tasks.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell directly to consumers through existing dealers, leveraging its engineering to differentiate the product from competitors, and capture premium margins on attachments.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to spend a few hundred dollars on a tractor for small‑garden use.
Deere can produce a reliable, affordable tractor that meets consumer needs.
Dealer network can reach and convert interested homeowners.
predictions: If offered a $200 garden tractor with basic mowing and tillage attachments, at least 10% of surveyed homeowners with small gardens will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales of the garden tractor will increase dealer revenue per customer compared to only selling farm tractors.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price the tractor as a premium, bundled product and sell accessories through dealers, capturing higher margins and building a consumer brand.
assumptions: Suburban homeowners value convenience and time‑saving in yard work.
Deere can design a tractor that is easy to operate and store for small‑garden use.
Dealer network can communicate convenience benefits effectively to potential buyers.
predictions: If a survey shows that at least 15% of homeowners with small gardens rank "convenience" as the top reason for purchasing a yard tool, the adoption rate for a bundled tractor will be higher than for a basic mower.
Sales of the tractor will be positively correlated with advertising that emphasizes time‑saving benefits.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are homeowners with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) who have never owned a lawn and garden tractor. They are shown two product concepts: (1) a $200 garden tractor marketed as "inexpensive, practical for a variety of chores" (aligned with T1); (2) a $200 garden tractor marketed as "convenient, time‑saving for yard work" (aligned with T2). Participants indicate intent to purchase (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. The survey also asks about current yard‑
X1.sample: 200 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region. Targeting homeowners who have expressed interest in gardening or yard work.
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each concept; difference in average intent between the two concepts.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average purchase intent for the "inexpensive, practical" concept will be at least 10 points higher than for the "convenient" concept, because homeowners prioritize low cost over convenience.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average purchase intent for the "convenient" concept will be at least 10 points higher than for the "inexpensive" concept, because homeowners prioritize time‑saving over price.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between the two concepts is at least 10 points, the theory that predicts the higher intent for the corresponding concept is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, both theories remain uncertain.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate whether homeowners prioritize inexpensive practicality over convenience. If the survey shows a ≥10-point difference in purchase intent favoring the "inexpensive, practical" concept, proceed to develop a consumer offering; otherwise, maintain focus on the B2B dealer model.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) who have never owned a lawn and garden tractor and are interested in gardening or yard work.
final.value_proposition: A $200 garden tractor marketed as "inexpensive, practical for a variety of chores" sold through existing dealer network, leveraging Deere’s engineering to differentiate from competitors.
final.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within 12 weeks, using €15,000 of the €20,000 test budget.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on homeowner purchase drivers in 1962.
would_change_if: If the survey shows a ≥10-point difference in purchase intent favoring the "convenient" concept, T2 would become the favoured theory and the recommendation would shift to develop a convenience‑focused offering.
If the survey shows no significant difference or a result that does not support either theory, the recommendation would remain unchanged and further testing would be needed.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are homeowners with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) who have never owned a lawn and garden tractor. They are shown two product concepts: (1) a $200 garden tractor marketed as "inexpensive, practical for a variety of chores" (aligned with T1); (2) a $200 garden tractor marketed as "convenient, time‑saving for yard work" (aligned with T2). Participants indicate intent to purchase (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. The survey also asks about current yard‑
arguments.sample: 200 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region. Targeting homeowners who have expressed interest in gardening or yard work.
arguments.measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each concept; difference in average intent between the two concepts.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average purchase intent for the "inexpensive, practical" concept will be at least 10 points higher than for the "convenient" concept, because homeowners prioritize low cost over convenience.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average purchase intent for the "convenient" concept will be at least 10 points higher than for the "inexpensive" concept, because homeowners prioritize time‑saving over price.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between the two concepts is at least 10 points, the theory that predicts the higher intent for the corresponding concept is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, both theories remain uncertain.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they perceive them as a practical, inexpensive tool for multiple tasks, and they can purchase them through existing dealer networks without requiring new channels.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly increasing small‑garden households need a tool that can handle multiple chores; the tractor's low price and ease of use make it attractive compared to manual tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging existing relationships and avoiding the need for new retail channels.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.

Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price tractors modestly and sell accessories, earning revenue from a new consumer segment while leveraging existing tractor engineering.

Deere can reach this segment through existing dealer network or new direct channels.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Homeowners
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are homeowners with small gardens (defined as under 1/4 acre). They are shown a basic lawn and garden tractor (similar to 1963 model) and asked: "Would you purchase this tractor for occasional yard work if priced at $500?" (price reflects 1962-63 consumer price level). They also rate perceived usefulness (1-5) and convenience (1-5).
X1.sample: 200 homeowners recruited via gardening forums and local community boards, balanced for age, gender, and region.
X1.measure: Proportion of participants who indicate "Would purchase" at $500; average usefulness and convenience ratings.

prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of participants would purchase at $500, indicating demand driven by convenience and low-cost entry to yard work.

final.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) who need occasional yard work and value cost-effective, multi-use tools.
final.value_proposition: A basic lawn and garden tractor priced modestly (e.g., $500 in 1962 dollars) that is easy to use for multiple tasks, sold through existing dealer network or new direct channels.
final.next_action: Run the willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) within 12 weeks, targeting 200 homeowners recruited via gardening forums and local boards.

arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are homeowners with small gardens (defined as under 1/4 acre). They are shown a basic lawn and garden tractor (similar to 1963 model) and asked: "Would you purchase this tractor for occasional yard work if priced at $500?" (price reflects 1962-63 consumer price level). They also rate perceived usefulness (1-5) and convenience (1-5).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.claim: Small‑scale farmers will purchase tractors directly from Deere because they need specialized equipment for specific tasks and trust Deere’s engineering.
T1.who_benefits: Deere benefits by selling tractors directly to farmers at premium prices, bypassing dealers and capturing higher margins.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Farmers gain access to Deere’s proven tractor technology and service support, reducing reliance on dealers and perceived savings.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors at higher retail prices and retains control over the sales channel, limiting dealer markup and potential price erosion.
assumptions: Small‑scale farmers have sufficient capital to purchase a tractor directly.
Deere can service and support tractors sold directly without major infrastructure changes.
Trust in Deere’s brand and engineering outweighs dealer presence for this segment.
predictions: If Deere launches a direct‑to‑farmer offering, purchase rates among small‑scale farmers will increase compared to existing dealer model.
Deere will achieve higher average transaction value per tractor sold directly.

assumptions: Homeowners have sufficient disposable income for a tractor purchase.

predictions: If Deere launches a direct‑to‑consumer offering, purchase rates among homeowners will increase compared to the existing dealer model.
